extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy (philosophy of mind/biology), scholars of Bergson
extracted.subtask_description: Close philosophical analysis distinguishing 'instinct' and 'intelligence' as two complementary but divergent modes of psychical activity, focusing on their objects, consciousness, functions, advantages, and limits. The chapter frames these differences in terms of action (tools/instruments), knowledge (matter vs form/relations), and the intellect's practical adaptation to the material world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct and intelligence are complementary but different
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinct and intelligence accompany each other only because they are complementary, and they are complementary only because they are different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctions will be drawn sharply (diagrammatically) for clarity, though in reality the two tendencies are mingled in concrete cases; expect idealized outlines that must later be softened to match living complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence as the faculty of manufacturing artificial objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence, considered in what seems to be its original feature, is the faculty of manufacturing artificial objects, especially tools to make tools, and of indefinitely varying the manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical invention is central to human intelligence; social life and historical epochs are shaped by the manufacture and use of artificial instruments (e.g., steam-engine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct perfected: faculty of using (and constructing) organized instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinct perfected is a faculty of using and even of constructing organized instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many animals the instrument is part of the body (made/maintained by organization), and instincts often reflect the continuation of organizing processes; examples include insect polymorphism and species-specific specialized actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core distinction: organized (instinct) vs unorganized (intelligence) instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinct perfected is the faculty of using and constructing organized instruments; intelligence perfected is the faculty of making and using unorganized instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organized instruments are integrated with the organism and act immediately and perfectly for specific ends; unorganized/artificial instruments are made of inorganic matter, require effort, and enable wider, variable uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and drawbacks of instinct vs intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinct's instruments act at once with often wonderful perfection but impose specialization and limited adaptability; intelligently constructed instruments are imperfect and effortful to use but can take any form, serve many purposes, and extend the organism's powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instinct secures immediate success with little internal change; intelligence risks more but yields expanding liberty and new needs—its benefits grow as construction becomes more advanced (e.g., tool-making breeds further needs and social change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness defined as difference between potential and real activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The consciousness of a living being may be defined as an arithmetical difference between potential and real activity. It measures the interval between representation and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When action perfectly matches representation (habit, somnambulism), consciousness can be nullified; consciousness is intense where many possible actions are indicated without decisive action (hesitation/choice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of consciousness to instinct and intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinct tends toward unconsciousness because representation is 'stopped up' by action; intelligence tends toward consciousness because it is essentially a labor under difficulties — a deficit between representation and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciousness often appears as an accident in instinct when an obstacle thwarts automatic action; conversely, consciousness is more intrinsic to intelligence since inventing involves choosing among alternatives and encountering obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innate knowledge: instinct knows things; intelligence knows relations (forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever, in instinct and intelligence, is innate knowledge, bears in the first case on things and in the second on relations. Instinct implies the knowledge of a matter; intelligence, in so far as it is innate, is the knowledge of a form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a newborn's immediate knowledge that locates a particular object (instinctive); a child's immediate grasp of relational categories like attribute-to-subject or verb relations (intelligent/formal). Instinctive knowledge is categorical; intellectual knowledge is hypothetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellect adapted chiefly to the unorganized solid (discontinuity and immobility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our intelligence, as it leaves the hands of nature, has for its chief object the unorganized solid. Of the discontinuous alone does the intellect form a clear idea. Of immobility alone does the intellect form a clear idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intellect favors treating matter as divisible units and immobilities assembled to represent movement; fluidity and living variability escape the intellect's natural scheme because fabrication and practical manipulation require stable, discrete elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence treats matter as carveable and substitutes immobilities for movement
rubrics_metrics.description: An intelligence which aims at fabricating is an intelligence which never stops at the actual form of things ... it regards the matter as indifferent to its form; it makes us consider every actual form of things as artificial and provisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fabrication the mind imagines endowing various kinds of matter with the desired form; this practical tendency legitimizes representing movement by assembled immobile parts (a practical equivalent rather than true reconstitution of movement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and divergence: some things only one faculty can seek/find
rubrics_metrics.description: There are things that intelligence alone is able to seek, but which, by itself, it will never find. These things instinct alone could find; but it will never seek them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the life-force is limited, instincts and intelligence diverge in evolution: instinct finds particular, intimate objects; intelligence supplies formal, general relations—each has unique capacities and blind spots; neither completely subsumes the other.
